utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Prosecutor [sic]. Do I take it that the appearances are the same as yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the addition of Julia Lee and Ozren Jungic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours for the Defence, Branko Lukic, Miodrag Stojanovic, Milos Saljic, Dan Ivetic and Erica de la Harpe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That's the new addition for the day. Good. Welcome. Yesterday we were busy talking about the admission of associated exhibits, Mr. Lukic, and you were saying you were objecting to the admission of all of them. Could you please just, in a -- in brief state what the basis of your objection is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we said yesterday, we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you carry on, just to say for the same reasons as yesterday and the day before, the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we said yesterday, we don't know what we have on those videos, if we do not ask the creator of the video what, on that video is. We showed two videos that are different from what we had announced that we have on those videos. So if the videos are not explained, we think that they don't have any probative value for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lukic, any -- the jurisprudence around the associated exhibits is that they are associated because they are discussed in the statement. Is that not the jurisprudence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But probably it is more for written exhibits, how we understand it. Because video is completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't -- I -- you would have to cite me to the authority which says it is just for written exhibits, because as I understand the jurisprudence it just says that any exhibit is an associated exhibit if it is discussed in the statement, and I don't hear you saying that they are not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They are discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that discussion should tell us what the videos are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But another issue we had yesterday and probably we will have in the future, since those videos were time-consuming, we didn't have time. Otherwise, I had all those videos prepared. If I had time I would go through every single video and discuss it with the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like us to mark them for identification and give you time to go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If can you call the gentleman back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. That's not -- calling the gentleman back has got nothing to do with giving you time to look at the videos, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I saw the videos, all the videos and I have questions for them. I have written questions to go through, the videos to go with the -- Mr. Van Lynden and ask him about the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not following your argument now. At page 3, you say: "But another issue we had yesterday and probably we will have in the future, since those videos were time-consuming, we didn't have time" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- "otherwise I had all those videos prepared. If I had time I would go through every single video and discuss it with the gentleman." And then you are saying ... then you then say, "If we can call the gentleman back." But I thought you are saying you haven't had time to go through the videos to determine in fact whether you do want to cross-examine or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to go through all the videos here during the trial. Otherwise, of course, I -- I saw all the videos given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. I see. Oh, that's your problem. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution's position is, is that the videos do in fact meet the legal test for admission as an associated exhibit. I am not aware of any exception with respect to video material. With respect to Mr. Lukic's submission now that he would have appreciated an opportunity to examine the witness on these videos, my submission is that that is something that should have been raised before the witness has been discharged. Having said that, I would inform the Chamber that the witness lives here in The Hague just a matter of a few blocks from the Tribunal if the Chamber should decide to grant what sounds like maybe an application to recall the witness at some future time to examine him about specific videos that could be done without significant inconvenience to the witness. But I submit that Mr. Lukic, if that is his application that it probably is best done in writing so the Prosecution can evaluate it and the Chamber has more detailed information about the application before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that, indeed, your position, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is the case, then will you do that in writing so that the Prosecution can respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the meantime, we can MFI the exhibits. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't have no problem with MFI'ing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me for numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, we have got the numbers. We just wanted to know if we can be MFI them. Madam Registrar, if they may be MFI'd, please. Do we need to call them out? Not necessary. You can do that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assign only a range -- a range of numbers and then [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So exhibits will receive numbers from P80 up to and including P89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Groome, I guess you want to hand over to Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a matter I would like to raise with the Chamber before we call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. If you may, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday the Chamber raised the issue of Mr. Mladic's conduct during the hearings with Mladic Defence and the accused himself. I would like to make the Chamber aware of the Prosecution's position with respect to this matter. Mr. van Lynden testified Tuesdays and Wednesday of this week. At several times during the course of his evidence, Mr. Mladic hurled insults at the witness. These were not recorded on the transcript but did go out on the video feed on the proceed and were reported both by local and international press. I spoke with Mr. van Lynden after he testified and after he was discharged as a witness to thank him. He had read about these reports on the Internet and was quite displeased that a witness would be subjected to such behaviour in a court. And I convey that the Court now. After the second session on Tuesday, I asked a member of my staff, a B/C/S speaker, to listen to the B/C/S channel. During the third session, a particularly vulgar insult was shouted out by Mr. Mladic. This has not yet been reported in the press. I must say that the Prosecution did not anticipate such behaviour from a senior military officer. The Prosecution appreciates the Chamber's attention to this matter yesterday. Last evening I reviewed the Chamber's decision of the 15th of August, 2012, and noted that the Chamber has only authorised a recording of the video image of Mr. Mladic. There is no provision for recording what he says. I recognise that ordering a microphone be left on to record his statements might have implications for his ability to confer with his Defence team, and, thus, the Chamber might have refrained from ordering such, in light of this. The Prosecution will consider its position further. Hopefully after yesterday's admonition by the Chamber, Mr. Mladic will conduct himself with the dignity expected of an officer. If not, the Prosecution will be applying for additional measures to protect future witnesses from having to listen to insults while giving evidence. Secondly, Mr. Mladic has also adopted a practice of shouting instructions and other information to his Defence team. We can all hear it and many members of the Prosecution team understand what is being said. Before the summer break, Mr. Mladic said something which was certainly not in his interests to say. I want to make it very clear to Mr. Mladic and the Mladic Defence that while communications between an accused and his counsel are privileged and sacrosanct, it is the Prosecution's position that if such communications are made public, because they are shouted across a courtroom, it is the Prosecution's position that this important privilege may be deemed to have been waved and the Prosecution may seek to use any inculpatory statements shouted in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I may just add it is not deemed to be waived. It is waived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Chamber has clearly demonstrated that it will allow Mr. Mladic to consult with the Defence team whenever necessary and in a way that protects the privacy of these communications. It is important that Mr. Mladic and the Defence appreciate that the Prosecution, if this conduct continues, make seek in the future to introduce such statements. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we will. I think we will have, Your Honour, especially regarding the turning on the microphone, but if you can give us some time probably we should answer to this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. I want to say to you, Mr. Lukic, that if some members of the Prosecution could hear the insults coming from Mr. Mladic, I would expect that all of the members of the Defence have heard them, and I would have expected them -- on their own volition to have taken action to stop Mr. Mladic. We haven't done so as the Bench because we don't understand what he says. You do. And I want to say to you on a preliminary basis, prima facie view, the Chamber takes a dim view of the conduct of the Defence in that they have not intervened when their client has spoken in the manner alleged by the Prosecution. It is a preliminary view. Have you the right to argue and show that, in fact, you didn't hear him. Later, as you say -- you will attend to this later. Okay? Thank you. To you, Mr. Mladic, I just want to say: Stop your fingers. I want to talk you. Okay? You stop misbehaving. This is a court of law and you shall behave yourself in the manner in which you are expected to do, and if you do not, this Court does have measures it can take to deal with the situation. I hope you understand that. Before we hand over to Madam Bolton, one last point from the Bench. And this relates to CLSS B/C/S translation policy, which arose in relation to Exhibits D27 to D37. In relation to these exhibits which were tendered through Witness Schmitz for which a B/C/S translation is missing, the Defence -- Mr. Mladic -- the Defence submitted that it could not approach CLSS for a B/C/S translation. There has been further research into the issue of CLSS policies on providing B/C/S translations to the Defence. The Registry Court Officer has informed the parties of the exact procedures. If there are further problems, the parties should first seek a resolution with the Registry and only as a last resort revert to the Chamber. The Chamber further reminds the Defence to provide ... I don't think -- no, no, sorry. I will leave it at that. I think the Chamber is satisfied that where the Defence does not need any B/C/S translations, the languages of the Court are satisfied. Thank you so much. Mr. Groome, is that now Ms. Bolton's turn?

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

Adjudicated fact 1713 and 1714 which relate to the shelling of the old town area of Sarajevo in early May 1992. Also, adjudicated facts 1693, 1697, 1698, and 1699, which deal with the issue of the erection and dismantling of barracks in Sarajevo on March 1, 2nd, and 3rd, 1992, following the announcement of the referendum on sovereignty.

utterances.text: Oh, I was going to ask a question. I see a pseudonym is assigned to Mr. Doyle and I also noted that there are no protective measures with respect to him. Is there any reason why we -- he should be referred to by pseudonym?

utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm best placed to answer that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, every Prosecution witness has been assigned an internal RM number for internal reasons and also to facilitate communication. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Doyle was a member of the Irish armed forces. From October 1991 until August 1992, he was deployed to the former Yugoslavia. During that time-period he served in three different capacities. In October and November 1991, he was a monitor with the European Community Monitoring Mission, or ECMM, and he was stationed in Banja Luka. On the 24th of November, 1991, he was promoted. He remained in the employ of the ECMM but became the head of mission in Sarajevo region and at that time he was transferred to Sarajevo. While serving in that capacity he had a -- 65 international monitors reporting to him. They were stationed in different areas in the former Yugoslavia and those areas included Bihac, Banja Luka, Tuzla, Mostar, and Sarajevo. His responsibilities as head of mission included liaising with political, military, religious and community leaders. This included having contact with the president of Bosnia, Mr. Izetbegovic. He had contact with a number of members of the JNA, or federal army of the republic of Yugoslavia. He had contact with Radovan Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Nikola Koljevic. He completed his work with the European Community Monitoring Mission at the end of March and he was then approached to act as Lord Carrington's personal representative and he commenced working for Lord Carrington on the 10th of April, 1992, and Lord Carrington was the head of the International Conference for Peace in the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Doyle will give evidence about his observations of the rising ethnic tensions in the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and particularly near the Croatian border in the fall of 1991, and he will give evidence that one source of that tension arose from the mobilisation order that was issued with respect to the JNA. It was the position the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the order, in essence, was not to be responded to. They took a neutral position on it. And, as a result, most Croat and Muslims did not enlist or answer the call-up, whereas, the Serb population did mobilise. And I anticipate that the witness will tell that you in the municipalities, the JNA were taking weapons that had been stored with local territorial units, defence units, and then giving those to the reservists who were answering the mobilisation. And the net effect then was that the Serb population in Bosnia was becoming armed, and the other populations were not. As I indicated, the witness left the municipalities at a certain point, and although he continued to receive reports about the goings-on, he was himself stationed in Sarajevo from that point forward, and he will have evidence to give about the situation in Sarajevo. He has some evidence to give about his own observations of the forcible transfer of non-Serb populations in parts of the Serbian-held areas of the city and about rising tensions in the wake of the referendum results and, ultimately, the outbreak of violence. He has some evidence to give about the bombardment of the city of Sarajevo, particularly in May 1992 and his observations of artillery in the hills around Sarajevo and also about the transfer of weapons from the JNA to the Bosnian Serbs. That's the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I just have a technical issue. A brief indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, your statement was taken back in 1995, and I just wanted to ask you a little bit about what you have been doing since 1995. I understand that you remained with the Irish armed forces until you retired in 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at that time of your retirement what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand, sir, that after returning from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you held a number of different posts, which included, in 1995, being the commander of an infantry battalion stationed in Limerick?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were also a battalion commander with the UNIFL in Lebanon in 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: For a time period you were the director of public relations for the Irish armed forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you also served in different capacities with the UN training school and the Irish armed forces training centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In 2002 to 2004 you were the director of the reserve forces for Ireland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what are reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Reserve forces are the equivalent of territorials that will be taken up in the case of emergencies. They would be what we might term as part-time soldiers. They come up periodically on weekend for duties and for training so they would be there as a reserve in case the occasion would demand that they become part of the Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interprets kindly ask you to slow down and put a pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I'm going to interrupt you. The interpreters are asking that you slow down and pause in between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the comment of the interpreters you will not hear if you don't use your earphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I couldn't hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Precisely because you were not wearing your earphones. That is the point the Judge was making. You won't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, that was actually the question I was asking was what channel the interpretation is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Going back to 2004/2006 then, I understand that you were the Chief of Staff, military division, UN peacekeeping operations in New York?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you may, if you need to, refer to your statement to keep up with my questions, because I will be referring, at times to various paragraph numbers. At paragraphs 4, 5, and 6 of your statement, you talk a little bit about the mandate of the ECMM, and I have a few questions about that. You indicate that the mandate of the mission was to try to deter the spread of conflict from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina. My first question is: Do you have any experience up to that point in time in monitoring activities in conflict or crisis areas?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Personally, I served with the United Nations Truce Supervision Organisation which was monitoring cease-fires in the Middle East, so from 1984 to 1986, I was a United Nations military observer in Syria and thereafter in Lebanon. And then I was appointed to senior operations officer of Observer Group Lebanon. So, yes, I would have had experience in negotiations at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who were the parties to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, sorry, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I had no personal involvement in the actual operation in Croatia, but I was aware of the fact that we had monitors based in Zagreb who were covering the area of Croatia. They had been deployed to Split and from Split, teams were established to go out to various places like Dubrovnik and other centres. All of my deployment at that time in Yugoslavia was based in Bosnia-Herzegovina so it is in Bosnia itself that I would have had experience of dealing with various sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My question may have been a bit vague. Who were the two parties that were in conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the parties -- are we talking about Sarajevo? We're talking Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We're talking about Croatia when you were first assigned.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, when I was first assigned, as I said, I did -- there was no actual service that I carried out in Croatia. But at the time that I arrived I know that negotiations were in hand for the withdrawal of the federal army from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Which federal army?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The Federal Army of Yugoslavia commonly known as the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know with whom the JNA had been in combat in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had been in combat with Croats of Croatia and there were areas of Croatia which had large populations of Serbs particularly in the area called the Krajina, and that's where there was some conflict and the need for monitors to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did the Croats have an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats were attempting to establish an army. At that stage, of course, the Croats didn't have their independence so it was part of the federation of Yugoslavia whose army basically was the JNA. So at that time the Croats may have had some territorial forces that I would be unaware of but certainly didn't have an army as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, Madam Bolton, that's as far as we can take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 5 there's an indication that it was understood by all sides that if the conflict spread to Bosnia, it would make the Croatian conflict seem very small. Do you know why there was that feeling?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the feeling we had at the time was that such was the ethnic mix in Bosnia between Serbs, Croats and Muslims that if the conflict did come from Croatia, and it would be very serious, and it was one of the few issues that all sides in Bosnia actually agreed on. They all agreed when I met the political parties, the SDA, who were the Muslims, the HDZ, who were the Croats and the SDS with Serbs, they all agreed, Yes, we do know, Mr. Doyle, that if conflict comes to Bosnia it will be pretty serious, because the population of Serbs in Croatia in comparison to Bosnia was relatively small, but in Bosnia there was a considerable population of Serbs. So all sides agreed that if conflict were to come it would be very serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. Now I understand that when you were working as a monitor, so October, November 1991, one of your responsibilities was to prepare reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was done with the reports that you authored?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The format at the time was that various teams of monitors were deployed to different areas in Bosnia as you have mentioned earlier. And they would go out to the various municipalities which were called "opstina" and they would meet the various people who were in charge like the mayor of the town, the police chief, and then the party leaders in that local community. We would try and learn to find out what exactly are the concerns of the various communities. What are their fears? What are their hopes? And then we would then compile a report based on her findings. The difficulty we had at the time was that we didn't have good communications. So, for example, when I was in Banja Luka, the only means I had of sending reports back to the headquarters in Sarajevo was by using a fax machine belonging to the hotel that we stayed in. This, to me, was not a secure means of transmission of information, so a lot of the reports would have been held and either sent by fax, if we felt it would be safe, or else taken by the team when it returned back to Sarajevo after, say, a week's duty in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you say you didn't have a good communications you're talking about between the monitors in the field, as it were, and your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of the reports that you authored how important was it to you to try to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, my experience in any form of peacekeeping was that it is essential to maintain impartiality and neutrality. And, therefore, I would check all of the reports to make sure that they accurately reflected what we found out on the ground. The report then would be agreed upon by the three members of the team. The team I was a member of also had an officer from France and an officer from Greece. Because I was an English speaker, they looked to me, I think, to write the reports, but I wouldn't send the report unless they agreed with its content. So it was done by our experience. It was done by our -- our -- I suppose our professionalism in our training and then when we agreed with the content of the report, it would either be sent by fax, if we felt it was safe, or else it would be taken by the team returning to Sarajevo after its, we say, a week's tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. Moving forward in time when you become the head of the ECMM and you're sent to Sarajevo, did you continue to receive similar reports from your monitors?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. At that stage in Sarajevo, I had established an operational cell and the -- one of the tasks of the operational cell was to co-ordinate the reports from the different areas from Bihac, from Tuzla, from Mostar, from Sarajevo itself and then that operation cell would make out a consolidated or co-ordinated report and that report then would go from Sarajevo back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. And what was in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Zagreb was the then headquarters of the entire monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just moving forward into time, when you ceased working for ECMM and you became Lord Carrington's representative, did you continue to receive any information from the ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes one of the tasks I had from Lord Carrington was to attempt to keep the contacts I had, because at that stage I was relatively very well known by the leaders of various political parties, and therefore in order for me to be able to give an accurate report, I would look for information from the Presidency, for example. I would get information from some of the monitor teams of the -- of the ECMM, and then afterwards I would get some information from the United Nations force that was deployed. It was very important for me that one part of maintaining my neutrality was I did not look for military information because I didn't want to be targeted as some sort of an agent or a spy or informer or intelligence officer. And this is something I'd learned from my experience in the Middle East, that we don't look for hard military information. We didn't look for locations of units. We didn't look for weapons. But we did get the information about the trends, about the fears and anxieties were of the various population. So a lot of my information came from having the facilities of the monitor mission available to me when I was Lord Carrington's representative.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So if we could then ask some questions about the work you did when you were still a monitor in October, November of 1991. Now, at paragraph 7 of your statement, you've listed some of the municipalities that you visited while you were a monitor, and that list included Doboj, Banja Luka, Derventa, Prijedor, and others. Could you just tell the Chamber, please, what the atmosphere was like in those municipalities you've listed in terms of ethnic relations at that time.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I would have to say that one of the problems the monitor mission came across was that if we met with the party representatives all together we made very little progress because one side would refute what the other side was saying, and after a while we gave it some consideration and I made a recommendation that after I would say towards the end of October -- but -- about the end of October that there would be more gained by visiting the parties separately. So if we were to go to a municipality, out of courtesy we would meet with the mayor first, and if that mayor, for example, was a Serb then we would invite to meet the local Serb representatives of the SDS. And after that, we would then visit the Croats and the Muslims and then we would maybe talk, for example, with somebody like the police chief so that was the first thing we did there. The second thing, there were some common issues that seemed to come up in most of the municipalities. There was an increase in the amount of distrust and suspicion. Words began like Chetnik and Ustasha that were not used earlier, and there was a lot of reference back to what had happened in the Second World War. And we thought this was getting very serious. In addition to that, most of the areas we visited, the various party representative, certainly the Muslims and the Croats, were expressing concern about the amount of reservists that had been called up for military service, that in a lot of cases they were intimidatory. They were carrying weapons. They were creating a lot of fear amongst the non-Serbs. And this was an issue that I used to bring up myself when -- when I went on these visits. And one of them specifically is, Why does it appear to us, why does it appear that the Bosnian Serbs seem to have access to more weapons than those of Muslims and Croats? And, of course, we understood ourselves from the point of view that when mobilisation was called and the only -- the only ethnic group that obeyed with the mobilisation were the Serbs, we found out later that when they were armed by the JNA, and they finished their temporary service, they were allowed to retain their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've given us quite a bit of information there and I just want to break it down a little bit. You first -- you referred to a mobilisation being called. What was the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, my understanding at the time was that the federal authorities in Belgrade issued a mobilisation and that meant that citizens of Bosnia were expected to be called up to have military service with the JNA or alongside the JNA. The president, Alija Izetbegovic, objected to this and felt that this was not something that Belgrade should have the authority to do, so he made a proclamation at some stage that it was not mandatory for the citizens of Bosnia to obey the call-up to mobilisation. However, most of the Serbs actually did mobilise. So, on the one hand, where you had the federal army, which, at this stage, was interpreted as being increasingly pro-Serb, and the Serbs themselves getting armed from the JNA, we began to be concerned that the weapons coming in were all sort of on the one side. Sorry, I should add here that I took up the issue of the indiscipline of the reservists with all the JNA military commanders I met: The 5th Corps, the 9th Corps - not the 9th Corps. The 9th Corps was in Knin - the 10th Corps, the 4th Corps in Sarajevo. And these are issues that I brought up with the federal army myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just a few follow-up questions. You indicated that most Serbs responded to the mobilisation order. What about the Muslim and Croat populations?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I didn't -- I wasn't in a position to get exact figures but it was my understanding and what we were learning is that very few Croats or Muslims were actually being mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you also told us that when people responded to the mobilisation order, they were given weapons by the JNA and allowed to keep them. What understanding did you have as to where they were getting the weapons?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the clearest indication I had of that was when I went on a visit to Sokolac which is a suburb outside of Sarajevo, and I was meeting with a leadership of an internation conglomerate called SIPAD, and at that particular meeting, as I said, the normal thing was to visit then the local authorities, Serbs, Muslims and Croats, and at one stage in the middle of a meeting I could hear a lot of weapons being fired, and I turned around and I asked the question specifically, What is all the shooting outside. And I was told by the leader of the Serb party that these were reservists who had been mobilised by the JNA. They had carried out their period of service, they were now home, and they were letting off steam by firing their weapons into the air. And I asked the specific question, Are the weapons taken off these reservists when they finish their tour of duty? And I was told, No, they are allowed to keep them. And that trend seemed to be evident in other locations as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, you have explained, then, where the reservists were getting their weapons. You've told us they were getting them from the JNA. My question is: Do you know where the JNA were getting the weapons to distribute to the reservists?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't know specifically where they were getting them, but I mean, there was a very large armament industry in Bosnia, the largest in all of federal Yugoslavia so there was certainly plenty of weapons about -- so I'm not -- I can't in truth tell you exactly where the weapon is coming from, but we did believe that the weapons were being supplied let's say by the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, could you please slow down both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term Territorial Defence units within the context of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding of the Territorial Defence units were they were existing units that was part of the life in Yugoslavia all over the various republics, and those units comprised in Bosnia of Serbs, Croats and Muslims. And they had storage of weapons. And those weapons, I understood, after a while, were actually being used to actually arm the Serbs. So not only were they given by the JNA but they were taken from the various stores of the territorial units. And this, of course, was something again which was all one-sided.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you say that the Bosnian Serbs were taking arms from the territorial units, was there any involvement of the JNA in the seizure of those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misstates the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it misstates the testimony of the witness. He said the JNA was the one taking this as I read in line number 10 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Ivetic. Let just read ... Yeah. And your point being, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The counsel has now said "when you say that the Bosnian Serbs were taking arms," that is not what the witness testified to so I don't want counsel testifying about matters that are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, as I understand what's written in the transcript, he has said that: "... after a while, the weapons," sorry, "were being used to arm the Serbs but not only given by the JNA but taken from the various stores of the territorial units." So I understood the witness to be saying the Serbs were arming themselves from the territory units. Whereas, my friend thinks that what has been said is that the JNA was taking the weapons from the territorial units and redistributing them and I'm trying to clarify which was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think the best way to clarify that is to say to the witness: You say, Mr. Witness, that after a while, were actually being used to arm the Serbs. Who used to arm those Serbs? You should ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you answer His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: As best I can recall, the Serbs were being armed by weapons supplied to them by the JNA and also from stocks of weapons that were part of the Territorial Defence units that were held in stores.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who was accessing the weapons in the Territorial Defence force stores to arm the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I actually don't know. I suspect that it was probably the JNA, but I can't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You told us that your observations were that as a result of the response to the mobilisation order and the conduct of the JNA that the Serb population was becoming armed. Could you tell us what effect that had on ethnic relations in the areas?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, it caused a lot of concern because the Muslims and the Croats were becoming increasing worried, that these weapons might be used in the future against them. It was one of the consequences that probably was to their disadvantage by not -- to the disadvantage of the Muslims and the Croat by not obeying the call to the mobilisation. It meant they wouldn't have access to the weapons that the Serbs would, but they were quite willing to comply with the recommendation of the president when he said they should not actually go up for mobilisation. But it led to an increase in the tension in the areas, and because the relationships between the Serbs, Croats and Muslims was deteriorating, it increased their fears. That would have been my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. May I have 65 ter 02887.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, while we're waiting for the document to come up, this was a document that was for the first time noticed for this witness on August 20th, 2012 when the exhibit list for this witness was first given to the Defence. This document is not identified, to my knowledge, on the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosures for this witness that were made in February of this same year. And I would draw that to the attention of the Chamber that I view it as a lapse on the part of the Prosecution of their disclosure obligations under the Rules to provide adequate time and notice to the Defence of material that it intends to elicit through witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My understanding is this isn't a disclosure issue. My friend isn't saying he didn't have disclosure of the document. What he is saying is that when we filed our original 92 ter notice we did not include this document in that notice, which is correct. However, the practice has been before this Tribunal that - and there is no guide-line at this point in time that I'm aware of - that the parties exchange a final list of exhibits. Two days has been the practice in most of the Trial Chambers before the witness testifies. And the reason that there are obviously changes is that often you can't meet with a witness until a short time before they testify. It is only after meeting with the witness that you can ascertain, I think, that final list. So this list was actually provided more than two days ahead of time to my friend and, as I indicated, at this point in time that has been the practice followed with all the preceding witnesses without complaint from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution's position that documents can be sprung at least two days before they are used in Court, and that's fine. Is that what I understand you to be saying is the practice?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, for example, I recall before the Perisic Trial Chamber that our practice was two days ahead of time we had to provide a list of the -- final lists of the exhibits we intended to show a witness in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But these are -- these are documents that have been disclosed either under Rule 66 or Rule 68 or whatever other Rule or 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand my friend is indicating -- I don't understand my friend to be making a disclosure issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand him, he is saying it's late disclosure. It was given on the 20th, three days before the witness is on the stand. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The document itself, I don't know when it was disclosed. It's in the system. The document is in the system with all the other documents, millions of documents. However, in terms of this witness, the specific Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosures for this witness were done in February of this year and this document is not on that list of disclosures for this witness. The practice for the previous witnesses, it is true that Mr. van Lynden's exhibit list came four days before he testified, but he was from the first segment of witnesses, meaning that we had three months prior disclosure of the primary exhibits that were to be used with that witness. The same has been true for any other witness that has appeared thus far in this trial. This is the first witness for whom -- he was not on the first segment of witnesses and, therefore, there was no disclosure of an exhibit list for this witness prior to the summer recess of the Chamber. And, therefore, counsel has said that it is the practice in other cases. I have had several other cases at this Tribunal and we've had one week prior to witness appearing has been the rule. So I don't know. I do agree that this Chamber has not set a guide-line and that's why I bring this to the attention of the Chamber so that we can perhaps set some sort of guide-line on this, so we all know what the ground rules are for when exhibit lists are to be provided for witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do understand it, Mr. Ivetic, that you are not objecting to this document being tendered? Has it been tendered now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been tendered yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. But it is being used with the witness. You're not objecting to it being used with the witness right now. You are just seeking guidance from the Chamber as to how we will proceed in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Waiting for the transcript. Twofold, Your Honour. Yes, I'm seeking guidance, but depending on the questions asked for this witness, I may have other problems insofar as the Rule 65 ter summary for this witness does not necessarily cover all questions that could be asked of this document. But I will wait and endeavour to see what questions are asked of this document before making any general objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, shall we then wait until that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Bolton, you may proceed. Just before you proceed, Madam Bolton. We have now been sitting for 1 hour, 5 minutes. Practice in this case is that we sit for one hour and break for 20 minutes. Do you have a convenient point where you can stop?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, why don't I just put on the record a couple of comments I had and then we could break and deal with the document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The comments I have, Your Honour, are that this Rule 66(A)(ii) doesn't apply to this document. It's a rule that applies to a prior statements. The document is not a prior statement of this witness, and this document was disclosed in November of last year to the Defence. So this is really the only issue that's reigning is the issue of the fact that notice was given four days ago, I guess now, that we would be using it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When it was disclosed in November of last year, what was it disclosed as?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It was disclosed under Rule 68 (ii) which I would suggest is the appropriate Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 68 (ii). Thank you so much. Those are all the comments you would make?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all the comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, we're going to take a short break. We'll come back at 20 past 11. You may stand down and come back at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take an adjournment and come back at 20 past 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, may the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, I'm just conscious of the amount of time that we're using, and I'm going to ask you if you could try to keep your answers as succinct as possible. Going back to 65 ter 02887, if I may, please. Looking at the first page of this document that should be in front of you, sir. You see it's a document dated 20th March, 1992, and the author is Commander General Kukanjac. Did you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to, please, page 6 in the English and pages 4 to 5 in the B/C/S. Under subheading (5), you see some information indicating that some -- under subparagraph (f), the JNA had distributed some 51.900 weapons to volunteer units in the zone, and I'm wondering if that information confirms or contradictions your suspicions about the JNA's role in arming the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I think that would conform with what our suspicions were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would be asking to tendered that document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm confused if the -- if its being tendered -- the witness did not prepare it. I don't know if he has seen it before. He is not the author of the document. I don't have an objection to it coming in based upon the fact that a question was asked upon it, but is the document coming in as a whole or just as to the part that was presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's a document authored --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whole document or [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The whole document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] question that is being asked of the witness. What do we do about the whole document? If only asked one question about the document under 5 (f).

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think in fairness, Your Honour, that it's a report prepared by General Kukanjac, and in order to assess the reliability of the information that you should have -- and the context you should have the whole document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do we do that if we don't have General Kukanjac before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, in order to understand the context of the document the portion that is being proffered, Your Honour, I think you have to read the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 16, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, Madam Bolton, we have a guidance on that. You can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, it's 12 pages in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even that, we have clear guidance on tendering of exhibits where you just deal with one little sentence in a document of a number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours, and if pages 1 and the current page we're looking at under subsection 4 could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take page 1 and this page admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. And may they please be uploaded separately, Madam Registrar -- Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: They'll be uploaded, Your Honour, as 2887A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Of the two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2887A, once uploaded becomes Exhibit P97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 10942, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document that appears on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: That was done by my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And approximately what time-period?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I think this was done in around February 1992 to prepare for a visit of the head of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could move forward to the next page, please. The purpose of this document was to do what?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The new head of the monitoring mission was scheduled for a visit to Sarajevo. His name was Salgueiro from Portugal, and I prepared this document as briefing notes for his visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this document in its entirety if we could go to the last page, please - it's 19 pages, but I will indicate, Your Honour, that I will ask that only up to 65 ter 003322 -- sorry, this is an ERN. 00332219, which I believe is page 9 in the English version, is what I will be seeking to tender ultimately. And we'll have to have that uploaded into a separate document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just with respect to paragraph 49 and 51 of your statement, you indicated that by February 1992 the ECMM missions were having problems with freedom of movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, we were experiencing some problems there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in what areas?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Mostly, I recall, in the area of Banja Luka and north of Banja Luka which would have been towards the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could have page 5 of the document that's on the screen, please, in both English and B/C/S. Sorry, page 6 in the English and the B/C/S. Under the heading Bihac, second sentence says: "Access in the 9th Corps area is restricted." Do you know who the commander was of the 9th Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The commander of the 9 Corps at that time was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you know why they were having difficulties with access?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. But it was the monitor mission members from Bosnia who were not allowed into the 9th Corps area. I cannot speak for any of the monitors that would have been based in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with a General Ninkovic in this regard?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what did -- sorry, who is General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: General Ninkovic was the JNA commander of the 10th Corps in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what did General Ninkovic tell you about access to the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: He said that access would be denied by the commander of the 9th Corps to members of the monitor mission from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it your evidence, sir, that both the 9th and the 10th corps were billeted in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, my understanding was the 9th Corps would have been billeted in Knin and the 10th Corps billeted in Bihac or covering that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the 9th Corps has been discussed -- well, you say access in the 9th Corps area is restricted and this is under heading of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I put that down there because it was in the area of Bihac that I was given this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you for a clarification. In line 12 of the count page, you are recorded as having said: "I said that access would be denied by the commander of the 9th Corps." I said, or he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That should be he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Ninkovic, who was the commander of the 10th Corps intimated that permission would not be forthcoming from the commander of the 9th Corps to members of the monitor mission from Bosnia going into that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Seeking to tender the eight pages I alluded to into evidence, Your Honour. Again, we have to have it uploaded separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours. We have to consult with the client.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Correction, Your Honours, it is actually pages 1 to 9 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the Chamber still has a problem, Madam Bolton, because you actually used the first page and this page only.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the case of this document, however, it's a document that the witness personally prepared, the contents relate to him bringing up to date the mission on the -- the new mission commander as to what had been transpiring under the work of the ECMM. And, in my respectful submission, it does contain relevant information. I can ask more questions and deal with it in greater detain, but I'm conscious again of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note that Mr. Doyle is a 92 ter witness. Does he discuss the other pages in his 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. The contents of the report are discussed in his 92 ter statement. It was an annex, and originally we -- it -- it could have been proffered as an associate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you that you question --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at the time that the initial determination was made we had indicated we would not be, but we reserved the right to tender it if that changed. And in light of information that came out during proofing we decided to tender it, and therefore it could be, in my respectful submission, tendered as an associated exhibit. It is discussed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could it be or is it being?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, having not -- having not indicated previously we would be seeking to tender it as an associate exhibit I don't feel I can change that position. We've indicated or provided notice that we may try to tender it in court, and that is my position. It is discussed in the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I had understood it as being an associated exhibit, and since it is authored by the witness, I did not have an objection for this particular document being introduced in the manner that was foreseen for associated exhibits. The one issue I have that my client has just advised me of, while the witness answered the last question which related directly to Mr. Mladic, there was apparently a problem with the headphones and he did not actually receive that in a language he understood, so he was asking for that portion to be repeated insofar as it dealt directly with him and he did not have the ability to follow what was being said. But with respect to this document, we do not have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much Mr. Ivetic. Madam Bolton, are you able to get the witness to repeat the answer to the question that Mr. Mladic didn't receive in a language he understands that related to, I think, the fact that the commander of the 9th Corps was said to be going to refuse access to the area. And this was being said by the commander of the 10th Corps. If we can deal with that little part, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could just very briefly repeat what you told the Court about your conversation with General Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: When I requested General Ninkovic to find out if members of the mission from Bosnia could enter into the operational area of the 9th Corps the reply I received from General Ninkovic was that the commander of the 9th Corps, General Mladic would not allow or would not permit or give access to members of the monitor mission from Bosnia from going into his operational area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is that okay now, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm seeing nothing that says otherwise. So I believe that that's fine. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. The document is now admitted into evidence. The first nine pages of the document, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I receive just a number under which these pages will be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 10942A will receive number P98, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, sir, the point in time when you moved to Sarajevo, did you ever have occasion to stay at the Hotel Bosna?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The hotel I stayed in for the period of my time in Sarajevo was in Hotel Bosna in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at any point in time -- sorry. What kind of area is Ilidza who was the predominant [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Ilidza would have been a predominantly Serb area on the outskirts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you were first started staying at the hotel, what was the staff composition?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact breakdown but certainly there were Muslims and there were Serbs as members of the hotel staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you ever observe a change in that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was around the period when the dining-room was moved to the back of the hotel for safety so the conflict had actually started, and there seemed to be a new Serb delegation in authority in the area of Ilidza, and I was invited to a dinner that they were hosting and I noticed at the dinner that all of the regular staff that I had come to know were not there. So when I raised it, I was told that the Muslim members of the staff had been moved out of the hotel and had been dropped, as the word I learned was dropped off at the centre of Sarajevo. When I inquired as to why, I was told it was because it was for their safety because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who give you that information?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The -- I don't recall the name of the Serb, but he was the leader of the Serb delegation that was now stationed in Ilidza. I don't recall his name. I remember distinctly because I asked was there any Muslim member of staff who was retained, and he said, yes, the chef because he was a good cook was his reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You refer in your statement to paragraphs 83 and 85 to receiving a phone call from a Mrs. Banjac and she had expressed concerns to you about her husband who had been taken into custody by the Serb MUP in Vrace. And you indicate in your statement that you had raised the issue with Mrs. Plavsic and the Serb leadership on the 1st of May, and you were told that Mr. Banjac would probably be released very soon. I wanted to ask if there was any delay in your making inquiries about Mr. Banjac and your receiving that response from the Serb leadership. Did they need, for example, to step out of the room and make some inquiries or a phone call?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I raised it as a general issue when I went up to Pale on that occasion. And nothing had happened for a few days, and I raised it then by contacting Radovan Karadzic, and I was told that he would be released. I followed up on it by contacting this lady and she informed me that he had been tortured badly and that he was now a broken man physically. I had hoped at some stage I might meet with him but circumstances precluded that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We -- if I could have 65 ter 18738, please. Sorry, this is P0096 [sic] now. 00096. You recognise the transcript in front of you of a conversation between Mr. Koljevic and a Mr. Karasik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where do you recognise the transcript from?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The transcript was given to me by the acting prime minister of Bosnia at the time, a man called Musmir Mamusjehajic [phoen]. He gave me a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when was that given to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I think it was around the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, who do we say Mr. Koljevic is talking to?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh Mladjo Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a reference in the intercept to the withdrawal of some artillery. What was that in regards to?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: At the time this happened there were peace talks being held in Lisbon which were being attended by the party leaders. And in a conversation with Mr. Jose Cutileiro who was working as part the peace conference, I was asked if I would go to Pale to ascertain if the Serbs were complying with what they said they would do which was to withdraw some of the artillery from their firing positions overlooking the city of Sarajevo. So one of the reasons I went to Pale was to ascertain if this, in fact, was being complied with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when did you go to Pale?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I went to Pale on the 1st of May. I tried to get up on the 30th of April, but because there were so many military movements of heavy artillery and tanks on their way to Pale we were unable to get to our destination, so we returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Whose artillery and tanks were on the way to Pale?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: There were armaments from the JNA which were being given to the Bosnian Serbs in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just going back to the -- to the transcript, when you were actually given the transcript originally, were you able to listen to the accompanying audio at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, at the time that Mr. -- that the acting prime minister gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No. I was just given the transcript. I wasn't given any audio version of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And subsequently have you had the opportunity to listen to the audio?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked if I would listen to it again and if I could identify any of the voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you able to identify any of the voices?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was able to identify the voice of Nikola Koljevic but not the other person.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at that time were you given the opportunity to listen to other intercepts and do voice identification with respect to those as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I was asked to listen to maybe five or six different conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would ask for where this is located in the Rule 65 ter summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I have a brief indulgence, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps I could look for that shortly. I don't want to spend too much time just briefing -- I could either take a brief recess or I could continue on and come back to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Continue, and you'll come back to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I couldn't hear your response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Continue and come back to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You alluded a moment ago to a trip you made to Pale on the 1st of May, 1992. Who did you travel with?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I travelled with Mrs. Plavsic and another member of the monitor mission, Mr. Jeremy Brade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you have any conversation with Mrs. Plavsic en route?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What did she say to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: She spoke about the need for the Serbs to have their own territory and she referred to the fact that because Muslims were generally living in areas of the cities that the Serbs would need about 75 per cent of the territory in order to have their fair share. She also surprisingly mentioned to me that if this conflict were to take the lives of 3 million people, we might as well get on with it and carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At that point in time, May of 1992, what was the situation in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The situation was very tense. The issue of the referendum had been held, I think I would say that positions were being very much entrenched, and there was a lot of artillery being fired on the city. So movement was very difficult and quite dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where was the artillery being fired from?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: We were satisfied that the artillery was being fired from the area of Pale and the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you describe the quantity of -- of fire that you were encountering?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the exact details, but they were sufficiently frequent to force us into -- to take some cover in the bunkers; in my case, in the bunkers of the United Nations headquarters which were the PTT building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've described artillery being fired into the city from the surrounding hills. Did you observe any outgoing fire from the city towards the hills?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Not that I could discern.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I understand from your statement that a decision was made to withdraw the ECMM monitors from Sarajevo on the 11th of May, 1992 and that you were to be also evacuated at that time, on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How were you evacuated from the city?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was evacuated by a helicopter belonging to the JNA from Lukavica, and I was in the company of General Aksentijevic, the deputy commander of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Lukavica is a military base belonging -- or occupied by the JNA on the outskirts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you flew out by helicopter, which direction did you fly?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: We flew in a line generally from Lukavica towards Pale because I was informed by General Aksentijevic there was a requirement to pick up a member of the JNA who was very seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And as you flew out in the direction of Pale, can you tell us what you observed?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was able to observe a considerable range of artillery, heavy mortars and tanks that were on the ridge line between Sarajevo and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you form any opinion or conclusion as whose artillery, heavy mortars, and tanks those were?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that because we were on our way to Pale that they were belonging to the JNA or the Bosnian Serbs, and also the fact that it was a JNA helicopter. I felt that if it was belonging to anybody other than the Serbs they would have attempted to shoot down the helicopter I was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you flying at a range that you could have been susceptible to fire?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: We were flying -- we were flying at a range of maybe 2- or 300 feet. It was quite low.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were any shots fired at the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit P95, please. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: It is the report of a meeting I had with President Slobodan Milosevic in his office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At whose instance was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I understand the invitation to meet him came, in fact, from his office from a liaison officer of the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And before attending this meeting, did you have any conversation with your superiors about what role you would take in the meeting or what positions you would take?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I informed Lord Carrington of this invitation, and he asked me not to make any arrangements until they gave it some consideration and then I was issued with instructions after that long with the recommendation that I attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What instructions where you given?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was told that I was there mainly for a watching brief. I should listen to what President Milosevic wished to say to me, and I should accurately reflect in my report the points that he was to bring up. And then there were a few issues that I should, if the opportunity arose, ask him to do, which, I think, are generally listed on that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
