utterances.text: If I could have page 2 in both the B/C/S and the English. Paragraph 4 indicates: "I stressed that Lord Carrington was anxious for Milosevic to use his influence over Serbian irregulars in BiH and over General Mladic to end the shelling of Sarajevo." Was that something you were authorised to say?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And I brought that to the attention of the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could have page 4 in the English version, and also page 4 in the B/C/S. There's an indication at paragraph 7: "Milosevic pointed out more than once that Belgrade had vigorously condemned the shelling of Sarajevo which had been a futile and criminal exercise for which the perpetrators should be punished." Does this document accurately reflect what Slobodan Milosevic told you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who actually prepared the document?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The document was prepared by a first secretary to the British embassy who accompanied me to the meeting, and his task, I had asked him to report on what had happened as accurately as he could but not to be involved in any discussion with the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Final document I wish to ask you about, sir, is 65 ter 03344.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just been advised, Your Honour, that the B/C/S translation of this document is not yet available. I only wish to ask the witness about two sentences which I propose to read into the record so they will be simultaneously translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: First of all, could you tell us what the London Conference was?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The London Peace Conference was organised by, I think, the leadership of the United Nations and the British prime minister and all the leaders of the republics were being invited to see could they come to some arrangement to end the conflict in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could have, please, the next page, paragraph 5. There's an indication there that Dr. Karadzic said that he had issued instructions to "stop his forces from harassing those Muslims and Croats who were 'willing' to leave Serbian areas from signing papers to that effect. He confirmed that any such papers would have no validity in the light of a final settlement." Could you explain what that reference is to?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I think it was probably in relation to the fact that it was known that some non-Serbs were being expelled from their home -- homes and their estates, and they were compelled to sign a document, disavowing all ownership of those. I had an occasion to speak with Dr. Karadzic on this issue myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you remember what the date was that you spoke to Dr. Karadzic about the issue?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't have it actually in front of me, but I know it was during peace talks in -- in -- in Brussels, and it would have been -- I think it would have been in August 1992 because he requested to meet me over a photograph that I found in a national paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was that photograph of?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: It was a photograph taken of an emaciated prisoner in one of the detention camps in Bosnia which was given a lot of international coverage having been discovered, and I think the prisoner in the photograph was a man called Alic, Fikret Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall when the London Conference was?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment to find out, if I could. I think it was towards the end of August. Yes, the conference took place between the 26th and 27th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the peace talks in Brussels take place before or after the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: They took place before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll be asking to have that document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were going to read just two sentences out of it so that they can be translated, madam. Yeah, that's what I thought I heard you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I was seeking -- I suppose the translation is not yet available. If it could be -- I did read those two sentences and if it could be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To MFI or to admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03344 becomes Exhibit P94 [sic] marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, that was my penultimate document to ask you about, sir. The final document is 65 ter 01027.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you - while the document is being brought up - where was the headquarters of the ECMM located?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall the address?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: It was what we called, referred to as the Hotel I which I think was the international hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the headquarters have any official stationary that they used for correspondence?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: We had the logo of the monitor mission which was similar to the logo -- well, it was rectangle but it was the 12 flags of the then European Community, or now known as the European Union, and that was the logo we used on our headed paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where on your headed paper did that logo appear?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: As best I recall, it was probably on the top left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you have before you now a document, sir, and you've had the opportunity to review this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And based on your review of the document, does it appear to be an authenticity correspondence from the ECMM head of mission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that this is the document. I missed the number of the document, but I believe this is a document that is not on the exhibit list for this witness. It was not identified for this witness previously, and I believe the witness is not an author of this document so I can't -- I can't see the witness authenticating someone else's documents, and I would object to this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said you missed a number. The number that I saw is 01027. Are you able to identify it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am not -- then I can -- then I can correct what I said. It was first notice to the Defence on 20th of August, 2012, at 4.44 p.m. with respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. So it is similar to the earlier one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So what is your position now? You're just telling us that. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm also objecting to witness authenticating a document that he did not author and did not see previously to come into proofing. It would be a difference if it was a document he saw in the course of his duties, but my understanding of his testimony is he saw it for the first time in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The jurisprudence of the Tribunal allows, in essence, reliable evidence to come in and we often proffer documents simply through the bar table process and explain where we got the documents. The issue being one of authenticity, this witness is in position as a result of his role to examine the document and to give evidence about the fact that it appears to be an authentic document having reviewed it, and so, in my respectful submission, it should be completely admissible through this document. We certainly cannot call -- it has never been the practice of this Tribunal to call the author of every document before it is introduced. That would be an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has this witness been shown the name of the author at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: He has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can he be questioned through that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It won't be of assistance, Your Honour. I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name of the gentleman at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, at the end -- the person who signed it, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at that point in time, March 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was back serving in Ireland, in my home country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you don't even recognise the signature? You don't know this person [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. I assume this person was the head of the monitoring mission, but he was unknown to me, and I wouldn't have known who it was at that time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The other problem is that, Madam Bolton, the logo that you referred to on the left-hand corner of the document is black. It doesn't show the 9 -- I don't know whether you said the 9 flags or the 9 legs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the transcript said the 9 flags.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The stars. The stars of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, that's another problem. We don't even see that. We do see that it is typed "ECMM headquarters, Hotel I, Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. All I can say is that this witness has given his evidence with respect to the fact that it looks authentic, and it appears to be on the letterhead notwithstanding the fact that where the -- where he described the logo usually being located that it has not photocopied so that you can see the flags. Again, we proffer documents all the time through bar table motion without anyone saying anything about the apparent authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I understand the proffering of exhibits through the bar table. You are not proffering this one through a bar table. You are proffering it through a witness. Odd as that practice might be, that is the practice of the Tribunal. Where parties have failed to tender a document through a witness, they use the wake-up system of the bar table, which I find absolutely odd but that's what happens. Would you like to keep it until then?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point. And I simply didn't want us to be criticised for not having shown it to this witness who is a representative of the mission. We will seek to tender it through other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I make one point to clarify a number. It is recorded in - just a moment - page 55, line 24, that the document, 3344 becomes Exhibit P94. In my view that can't be correct, because P94 is a different document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said was P99 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the microphone was not activated. I was not sure if you had something to say. You mentioned Mr. Lukic's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I mentioned Mr. Ivetic's name. Madam Bolton has said she is turning the witness over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel Doyle, I have several areas I would like to ask some questions about today to try and better understand your testimony and to clarify some issues that you might have personal knowledge of. I will again remind you that since we speak the same language we both have to try and have a pause between question and answer and vice versa to assist those are that are translating these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add, you should both slow down while speaking. You're very fast speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I, for one, am aware of that, and I will endeavour to assist the translators in that regard as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I have some questions relating to your role in the European Community Monitoring Mission. You just talked about the headquarters being in Zagreb. What was the genesis of the decision to have the headquarters in Zagreb rather than in the capital of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would like to move to your role within the European Community Monitoring Mission. In your statement, you describe in paragraph 1 that you hold the rank of lieutenant-colonel after 30 years of service in the Irish Defence Forces. For the sake of establishing context, what rank did you hold in 1991 when you were first deployed to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I held the rank of commandant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you receive any promotions in rank or commendations relative to your deployment in the Balkans during the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of performing your duties with the European Community Monitoring Mission and later as a personal representative for Lord Carrington, did you ever have occasion to meet and/or speak directly with General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm waiting for the transcript and the interprets to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While acting in your role first as a monitor and then later as head of mission, were you acting in your military capacity; that is to say, were you subordinated and taking orders from your military superiors within the Irish Defence Forces, or were you taking orders from civilians?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was taking orders from the headquarters of the monitor mission. I was not taking any orders from my military headquarters in Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to yourself, how much briefing or training did you undergo before being deployed to Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I didn't receive any training, but we did receive some general briefings at Irish Defence headquarters. However, we were being deployed at very short notice, and I was one of the first to be deployed. So there was a question of time. It was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you quantify for us the amount of briefing that you received prior to deployment? Are we talking, days, hours, weeks? Any information you can give would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I would say it was probably a full day of briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of training or briefing to advise you of the unique constitutional framework of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina [Realtime transcript read in error "Yugoslavia"] which set it apart from other nations and, in fact, other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Again, I did not receive any training, but the briefing would probably have included those areas. But I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just -- I know that the witness has answered. But, Mr. Ivetic, how is the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia set apart from other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I said that, I misspoke, I was asking about the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now if I can ask you about the rest of the European Community Monitoring Mission personnel that were deployed into Yugoslavia, do you know if they had to undergo a similar type of training or briefing, as did you, prior to being deployed?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you at least know whether, prior to deployment, each member state of the European Committee had responsibility for providing its own personnel briefings or information prior to deployment?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't answer that in any great depth. I would suggest, of course, that it would be normal practice for people to be briefed by their home armies or departments prior to deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that -- as part of that briefing that you did receive -- or that you do recall, did it contain briefing of the conflict, as you called it, in Croatia? I think that's at paragraph 5 of your statement. You said your mission was to deter the spread of the conflict from Croatia. Did your briefing include instruction on the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: It would have included a general indication that there was conflict in Croatia with some of the details but probably no specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would your briefing have included an indication or appraisal of who was viewed as the bad guy in the Croatian conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I really don't think so, because, as I mentioned, I was one of the first Irish officers to be deployed. And, therefore, it was very early in this -- in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can find a convenient moment somewhere. I'm not saying right now. We're due out at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can -- we can could that now. I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Doyle, again, another break, another 20-minute break. Please come back at 20 to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 20 to 1.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, I now want to ask you, if you were -- at the time that you were first deployed to Yugoslavia spoke any of the local languages of the Yugoslavia with any level of fluency?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct then that you had to rely on translators for the performance of your duties?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who provided the translators? Were they from outside of Yugoslavia or were they locals?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Initially, the translators that -- or the translator that I worked with was provided by the authorities in Banja Luka, because that's where I was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct then that as you performed your duties you relied upon translators that were provided by either the SDA or the SDS, that is to say, local officials? Or was there a professional corps of translators affixed --

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The first translator I had was a Serb. He was a businessman from Banja Luka. I don't know whether he was a member of a political party or not; I don't know. Afterwards, the monitor mission started to pick some of their own people that they selected themselves rather than having people supplied. I think it differed in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I see we still have your statement up in e-court, if we could stay with that. In paragraph 13 of your statement - and you're welcome to follow along in your hard copy - you state there that: "On 13 October the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, in a unilateral statement declared a state of neutrality. This meant that the mobilisation was not authorised by the Presidency. The Serbs within the parliament did not accept this situation, and the Serbs within Bosnia continued to be mobilised?" The first question I want to ask you to clear things up, when you say "unilateral" here in your statement, does that mean that the rest of the Bosnian collective Presidency did not join Mr. Izetbegovic's position?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't think I can actually answer that because I don't know. I would assume that because the Presidency was divided ethnically, with different members, that there may have been objections. But the fact that he announced this as the President of the Presidency, I would have assumed that it had been discussed within the Presidency itself. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I -- I assume that when you talk about the divided ethnicity of different members, when we talk about the collective Presidency, during this time-period at least, we're talking about Ms. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Fikret Abdic, Mr. Stjepan Kljuc, Mr. Franko Boras, and Mr. Ejup Ganic. Is that your recollection as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your briefing and preparations for deployment to Yugoslavia, did your briefing cover the constitutional makeup of this seven-person Presidency and/or the rules of order and procedure for the same?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you, in the course of your deployment, either as a -- especially as head of mission, ever order any ECMM personnel to ever research the legal framework or rules of order of this collective Presidency and the methods of voting or official acts of this organ?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The briefings that would have been given to the incoming monitors would have included the makeup of the Presidency of Bosnia, but apart from that, rules of procedure, et cetera, would not have normally been included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you aware at the time that the -- that the head of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, that this was a rotating position that was to transfer to other members of the collective Presidency upon a stated term?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I actually don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that within the entire time-period that you were deployed in the -- in Yugoslavia that Mr. Izetbegovic remained at the position of the chair and that this was in excess of a year's time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 25 of your statement, you indicate that you were to maintain contact with the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of your official duties. Did maintaining contact with the authorities include keeping in contact with the other members of the collective Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in relation to the collective Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would like to ask you about 65 ter number 10944, which may have gotten a P number now. It's a Prosecution document and was annexed and -- it was originally was an annex to your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's P93, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P93. That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This document, as we wait for it to come up, I can give you the background on my question. This document, you will recall, is a statement from the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the beginning of March 1992. And if we turn to the first page, which we're at now in both languages, Colonel, do you recognise this report relating to the time-period, I believe, the 1st and 2nd days of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this wasn't raised in the direct, but this report was actually authored by yourself. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: This report was written by myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, your report gives the primary cause for tension in the area as the killing of a Serb and wounding of another at a wedding ceremony on 29 February 1992. And if we look down further on the page, at item E, there's a demand that the assassins should be caught: Two Muslim, one Croat. Sir, is it your recollection and am I correct that the reference to assassins here relates to the persons who attacked and shot at the Serb wedding that is it blamed for heightening the tensions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. Sorry, my microphone wasn't working. My friend suggested that the document indicates that the primary cause of tension was the shooting at the wedding, and that's not an accurate reflection of what is written in the document. It does indicate tension was heightened as a result of this, but it doesn't say it was the primary cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you do say primary cause at line 9 of page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do see that. Perhaps I can reformulate it and perhaps ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the shooting at the wedding was a significant factor increasing or heightening the tensions, as this report indicates?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I -- it was probably a factor, according to the Serbs. But in my profession, it was not the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if I can return to the question I had asked. Looking at item E, where it talks about assassins that should be caught and brought to justice, two Muslims and one Croat, am I correct that the assassins here relate to the persons who participated in the attack upon the Serb wedding?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. But I should add here that the word "assassins" wasn't my word. It was a translation of the exact demands that were laid out by the Bosnian Serbs. So it was their terminology, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough say. And, for the record, at this time barricades had only gone up in Sarajevo and were not up in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the other factor that you list, the referendum, had taken place on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page of your report, items A through G. And it's the second page on both languages, I believe. Would -- would you agree with me that this section is your verbatim recitation of the decisions reached by the Bosnian collective Presidency on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: As far as I recall, this is what -- these are the terms that were agreed. Whether they were implemented or not, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, we don't need to turn to the end of the document, but do you recall that the -- that an actual written statement was issued by the Presidency, which you attached to your report?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus on item B here before us. This reflects that the Presidency acknowledged that results of the referendum would not prejudice the structure of BiH currently under discussion -- under the auspices of the EC. These talks to continue as soon as possible. Sir, is the referendum that is being discussed here the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the talks or discussions that were under way as this indicates under the auspices of the EC, am I correct that these were discussions that were being undertaken in the Bosnian Herzegovinian National Assembly, or parliament, among the various Serb, Muslim and Croat elected officials?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is these were the discussions that would have been chaired by the peace conference rather than being discussed inside the parliament because the Serbs had already vacated the parliament and were not part of its structure anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the discussions in the peace negotiations, the Serbs were participating in that process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs were part of -- any time there was peace talks called, the Serbs were part -- party to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page of this document, we see at the end of the report you state that the decisions were reached unanimously by the Presidency. Does that comport with your recollection that all the members of the Presidency unanimously issued these statements?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if a voting process took place at this session prior to the statements being used?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now having used the term "unanimous" in this report, does that refresh your recollection when you earlier stated in paragraph 13 of your statement that Mr. Izetbegovic issued a unilateral statement, whether or not there's a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I really can't answer that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With regards to the mobilisation, I believe you indirectly inferred it in your testimony, but am I correct that anyone who did respond to the mobilisation, whether ethnically a Serb, Croat, Muslim, or one of the other ethnic minorities in Yugoslavia, received armaments as part of the mobilisation. Would you accept that statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I would accept that if they were mobilised that they would have been armed. Whether they would have retained them or not is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that as tensions developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, after the declaration of independence, that Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Abdic, and eventually Mr. Boras all stopped participating in the Bosnian collective Presidency?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I -- I can't say that for definite. At the subsequent talks, which I would have chaired, it was getting difficult for the Serbs to come to talks because, at this stage, they had moved to Pale. But we continued the normal negotiations by inviting them to attend, and some occasions they did, and many occasions they didn't. And we also include discussions with the JNA on this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Mr. Fikret Abdic? Isn't it correct he left for Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No. The very last peace talks that I was involved in Mr. Abdic was present. And that was leading up to -- attempting to get an agreement on the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia. My recollection is he attended those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did he continue operating as part of the collective Presidency?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I assume that he did. That would have been my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would the Serb members of that collective Presidency who were in Pale have continued to maintain their authority as members of the collective Presidency, in your opinion, as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: My opinion would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you or anyone at the European Community Monitoring Mission investigate the constitutional and/or legal framework to determine whether the authority of these members of the collective Presidency continued or ceased?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I should point out here that when I returned in mid-April to Bosnia, I was no longer a member of the monitoring mission, so I wouldn't have been party to what they were thinking on that. And in reinforce to the peace conference, I would have understood that people like Jose Cutileiro and Carrington would have been quite familiar with -- were trying to come up to a political solution. But I wasn't party to it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. If we could move onto another topic. Paragraph 28 of your statement, you talk about the Serbian autonomous areas and a briefing paper that you received on the topic. For the record, that was P98 which was used by the Prosecution. If we could call up P98 so the witness has that in front of him. Sir, am I correct that this briefing document does not contain any detailed discussion about the constitutional authority, authority under the Law on Defence, or any other Yugoslav or Bosnian law upon which the Serbian autonomous regions are said to be founded? Am I correct, therefore, that there was no research performed or that you had no knowledge of these aspects of these autonomous areas?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't have that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which aspects, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me break down the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't see any discussion of the constitutional bases or the bases in laws of Yugoslavia or the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for these autonomous regions discussed in this report or this briefing. Am I correct that there is no analysis of that performed by the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm a bit confused here. I don't -- is that document supposed to be in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it is. It is P number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P number 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 98. Yes. Briefing paper from the ECMM Regional Mission, Sarajevo, including information on the Serbian autonomous areas and mandate of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have the page that refers to the autonomous regions because I just have the cover here of it on --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't we turn -- I believe it's somewhere in the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would have been around February 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there an entity called the federal -- Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually can't recall at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On 7th April, 1992 is when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the EC. Is that correct sir?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So prior to that time, it would have still been part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a socialist federated republic under that republic -- under Yugoslavia. Is that your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The document that I have there does not go into any of the backgrounds on the issue of the autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, this is, I believe, the -- is this the second or the third page? Well, if I can ... Perhaps it might be easier to refer to your statement since you do mention this annex in your statement. Paragraph 28 of your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you talk about Annex 3 to this statement. Is this document that we just looked what was Annex 3 --

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't think so. This is a private document that I prepared, but there was a separate document on the establishment on the autonomous regions. That could be the document. I don't think that is the correct reference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, that was disclosed to us as Annex 3 of the statement, so I don't know ...whether there's another document that we have not been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, it doesn't -- my microphone keeps -- the light keeps flashing. It doesn't seem to be working properly. Is it working now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And there's another microphone next to you there, Madam Bolton, if that one doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. He may be referring what I think are pages 8 and 9 of the document, there's an annex, and I don't know if that's what my friend is looking for or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's best to show the witness those pages and see if that's what he was referring to when he mentioned Annex 3 in his statement, as I do not know. So that would be pages 8 and 9 of P98. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see pages 8 and 9 of P98, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now. That's the document, yes, I would have thought it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up. And now in this document, there is no analysis of the prevailing laws of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina upon which these Serbian autonomous regions were said to be founded. Am I accurate in that statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that there is no -- there's no detail as -- as you -- as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. To your knowledge, did anyone at the European Community Monitoring Mission research this topic or obtain a legal opinion on the same?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suppose you do have knowledge, since you do mention a crisis committee several times in your written statement, that the Bosnian Muslim SDA had also set up crisis committees during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. When I went into discussions at the time that -- of the referendum I was informed that a crisis committee under Mr. Ganic was sitting to come up with -- referring to some issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would now to ask you a little bit more about the referendum and the negotiations that you referenced on the topic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's future which you discuss in paragraphs 41 through 55, approximately. I'll take them one by one, but I wanted to give you an idea of where we are in your statement. At paragraph 46 of your statement, you describe how, on 30 January, Haris Silajdzic sought and received via yourself the assistance of the European Community Mission to run the referendum on independence. My question for you, sir, is that at the time of this decision to assist the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats on running the referendum, the constitutionality of the parliamentary vote had not yet been established, had it?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Can you -- I'm not sure I understand your question, sir. Can you -- can you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time that the European Community Commission had agreed to assist in the referendum, the parliamentary vote establishing that referendum had not yet been deemed constitutional by any legal body.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I sought a meeting with the judiciary of Bosnia on that -- on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Step by step. Am I correct that you were present for the parliamentary debate wherein the referendum issue was adopted by two parts of the body after the Serb delegates had left upon the meeting being closed. In your report, which is 65 ter number 10943, which is not an exhibit, so I think we should call it up. That's 65 ter number 10943. And if we could turn to the last page of that document. And, sir, there's a note there above a signature. First of all, sir, is this a document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this note wherein you -- wherein it is stated: "It is expected that the legality of the Assembly being reconvened after it was closed by the Assembly president may be questioned as may the authority of the president of the Assembly to conclude the session without a majority in the first place."

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, they're my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Am I correct that as you state in paragraph 43 of your statement on the 27th of January, you went to the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to try and get an affirmation from that court on the legality of this vote?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, to be fair, I'd like to supplement your summary from this paragraph of your statement with your actual testimony in another proceeding and ask you if still stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is transcript page -- Well, first of all, I think -- Your Honours, if I can have the instructions of the Chamber. I have this particular transcript in e-court, and I can show to the witness via e-court so that he has it in front of him. I do not intend to tender obviously a transcript from another proceeding as that would be voluminous. Would that method be appropriate, to have it on the screen while I read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Just that page would be appropriate. And if you would let us know in which case that was. Or let the witness know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. That is in the Karadzic proceedings on the 26th of May, 2010. Transcript page 2765 through 2766. And, Madam Registrar, that is 65 ter number 1D118. And it is page 76 and 77 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe your answer begins at line 17 in the middle of the page, sir. And if you just follow along with me, and I'll start by quoting: "I think to clarify this point, Your Honour, I would just like to say that at the conclusion of this marathon session of the Assembly, I compiled a report to -- to my headquarters and that report gave a general outline as I understood it to be of what the issues were. I was sufficiently concerned to put in that report the fact that according to the Bosnian Serbs there was a requirement for an agreement to be done by consensus, whereas, most of the people in the parliament seem to be going along the line of where they are going to pass a referendum if they had a majority. What that majority was, I wasn't sure [sic]. I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "But I did put down ..." -- And now we have to go to the next page to continue: "... that maybe this is something that needed to be checked out legally. So as a consequence of that, I sought a meeting with the supreme legal court, or whatever, of Bosnia, and I met with them the following day to find out whether or not the allegations by the Bosnian Serbs that this referendum debate was constitutional." And here, sir, am I correct that the argument would have been that it was unconstitutional. Is that your recollection? Is this an error in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: It would have been -- it would have been the assertion by the Bosnian Serbs that it was not constitutional because it wasn't an agreement by consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: And that's why I sought the meeting with the judiciary, to have them explain to me what their views were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the parts that we've read up until to you, do you agree that that is now - with the one correction - an accurate assessment of your recollections of this [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct that after having a meeting with the senior judicial bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they could not give you a definitive answer on the legality of this referendum?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct then that the assistance agreed to be given to Mr. Silajdzic was undertaken without any legal opinion as to the legality of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I know that the European Union agreed to assist the -- the process of -- of the referendum, so I -- I can't speak for the European Union on this. But I understand your point, yes, and I think that's a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any research being performed either as part of your mission or further up the chain as to this topic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You had already expressed your concerns to your superiors about the legality of this decision on -- to have a referendum. Can we then, therefore -- is it safe to say that someone overruled your concerns further up the chain?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I put my concerns in the report the concerns that I had that I refer to there. What was done with that, or how that was countered, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And we already talked about the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the European Community on 7 April 1992. At that time, was there any change in status as to the existence of a legal opinion about the legality of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And had there been any change expressed by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to amend their prior statement which you recorded in the document we looked at earlier from the 2nd of March, 2012, where they unanimously stated that the referendum could not prejudice the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you recommend to your headquarters or your superiors that at any point in time that the referendum was legal?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No. I simply felt my duty was to bring up the concerns that were being expressed. How they were dealt with or what final decision was made was outside my remit. So, according, I didn't make any recommendation of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 54 of your statement, you indicate that you had asked the members of the Presidency what would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be recognised. And you're quoted in your statement as saying: "The members of the Bosnian Presidency all said the same thing. They said that they believed the Bosnian Serbs would not be happy with this recognition but that they would come around to accept it ..." Am I correct that what you really meant to say here was that the -- that -- that you spoke with Mr. Izetbegovic and that he said these words?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You, in fact, did not have contact with the other Presidency members, did you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No. Except that I -- no, I had contact with Mr. Karadzic over this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And ... and the report that you sent to your superiors as to this -- or at that point in time it was Ambassador Cutileiro who was asking. The report you sent back to him would have clearly indicated that it was only Mr. Izetbegovic who had said that the Serbs would accept and that they would eventually accept this situation?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I remember distinctly mentioning Mr. Izetbegovic and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct then, sir, that -- that the recognition of -- well, strike that. You -- at what time did you leave the ECMM? That was March the 20th, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, around that time I returned to Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that time had the decision on recognition already been unofficially reached?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't actually recall. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever make a recommendation in regards to recognition?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your statement and your testimony, we've mentioned Mr. Alija Izetbegovic several times. Would it be a fair assessment to state that you had frequent contacts with either him or his office?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. Because there was a liaison office established to assist our mission which was based in the Presidency. So any time I would go down there, which was quite frequently, I would often meet the president. As, indeed, I would meet other members of the Presidency who had offices there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were also familiar with Safet Hadzic, the president of the Sarajevo Crisis Committee?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your contacts with Mr. Izetbegovic and other members of his office continue when you became Lord Carrington's representative on --

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In both of your capacities, both at the ECMM and as part of Lord Carrington's -- as -- advisor -- representative to Lord Carrington, did you have occasion to have contact with an individual by the name Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of Mr. Halilovic having been the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian Muslim armed forces that were -- at that time [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how -- well, you already said frequently. Let me ask you this question then, sir. In the course of your interactions with Mr. Izetbegovic, did you -- did you rely upon information received for them as part of your conclusions and, in particular, I want to direct your attention to paragraph 15 of your statement. That's the third page in English. And maybe I should read it, which part I'm focussing on. "The community was becoming aware that one section of the population, namely the Serbs, were becoming armed. The federal army was also becoming very much a Serbian army." And my question for you: Am I correct that this conclusion is part based on communications and information you would have received from officials, such as Mr. Izetbegovic and other members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. It would have come from the monitor mission primarily that I was the head of because we had teams deployed throughout the republic, and then it would come from various political members of the Presidency as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of clarity, when you say here "the community," are we talking here about the European Community?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that this assessment in paragraph 15 would have been applicable to the time-period up until approximately 20 March 1992 when you left that position?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. Because early in 1992, we -- the monitor mission was involved in monitoring the withdrawal of federal -- the federal army from Croatia, and the concern of the mission was that if the JNA was being withdrawn from Croatia, where were those JNA units going to end up and had that been agreed in Croatia itself, which I couldn't establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'd like to present to you some excerpts from the sworn statement of General Sefer Halilovic given to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996. It's in e-court as 1D00173. And I'd like to present you some aspects dealing from this time-period that we've just discussed in 1992 and relating to these same SDA officials who were -- or one of the sources for your conclusions in paragraph 15. At the bottom of page 2 in the English. Yeah, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This would be appear to be the French. I apologise. One moment. It appears that the French has been uploaded alongside the English. If we could turn to the 26th page in e-court. There we go. That's the English portion of this. And now if we could turn to the next page in the English. And at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could direct your attention to the last paragraph where General Halilovic says, and I quote now: "My work was approved by Izetbegovic himself, and on 2 December 1991, I presented my plan during a meeting in Hrasnica. At the meeting that day were: Alija Izetbegovic; two ministers, Munir Jahic and Resad Bektic; as well as the president of the Sarajevo Crisis Committee, Safet Hadzic, and his deputy Mirsad Kebo; plus Safet and Rahim Baltic and Suljo Kepidja." If we could turn to the next page because it continues just one line thereafter. I quote again: "During the meeting of 2 December 1991, in addition to the approval of my defence plan, another important decision was taken: Designations of the headquarters of the Patriotic League." Sir, first of all, do you recognise the names of these other officials who are indicated with Mr. Izetbegovic? Are any of them [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No. None of them were familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did, either in your time with the ECMM or later working with Lord Carrington, did the SDA officials that you had contact with ever talk about the Patriotic League or headquarters of the Patriotic League which they had established?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take it from that, sir, that you were not informed at that time that you were in Bosnia about the existence of a so-called Patriotic League founded by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: I was aware that there was an organisation called the Patriotic League, but the details of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down to the bottom of this page, I'd like to draw your attention, then, to some other factors. The last two lines on this page, going onto the -- going onto a couple lines on the next page: "It was obvious that the war was unavoidable, and on our side, in order to confront the situation, we were trying to secure weapons quickly at that time. "This [sic] task had been entrusted to Cengic Hasan, who was a member of the General Staff of the political branch of the Patriotic League, as I have told you. In order to carry out that task, he had set up a group of people responsible for supplying us with weapons. The group had succeeded in obtaining some on the black market in Croatia, Slovenia, Hungary, and Germany. And according to what I can imagine, this was made possible through funds which arrived from abroad, particularly from the countries of the Middle East with which Cengic had relations." Colonel Doyle, in the course of performing your duties, did Mr. Izetbegovic or anyone else at the SDA advise you about the activities of Mr. Hasan Cengic and the funds coming from abroad for the SDA to obtain weapons?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: The only thing I can say about that is that Mr. Ejub Ganic was the only member of the Presidency to come to me and say that the Muslims were desperate to get some weapons because they were completely out-armed, we'll say, by Serbs. In other words, I was very conscious of the fact that there was a desire by the Muslims to get weapons because access to them, weapons was very difficult to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: But the details here I'm not familiar with, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the third paragraph from the bottom. This is, I believe, the last part I want to show you from Mr. Halilovic's sworn statement, so please bear with me, sir. "Izetbegovic is the one who personally authorised Cengic to do the work of supplying us with weapons. He could do whatever he wanted, and since secret business deals were involved, no accounting records were kept on the Bosnian side. In this way, tens of millions of dollars transited through Cengic's hands without any type of control whatsoever. "Throughout the initial period of our defence restructuring, that is, starting from December 1991, and continuing until the beginning of April 1992, Cengic was able to organise the arms deals from which he made enormous personal profit [sic]. No one could oppose him because he had the moral backing of Izetbegovic." Colonel, did Mr. Izetbegovic or any of the SDA officials ever brief you or advise you that they had, already, as of December 1991 undertaken a campaign to obtain weaponry which involved tens of millions of dollars?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that at the time you were giving your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor and, in particular, paragraph 15 of the same, you did not have this -- any of this information?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such information about steps taken to arm one side of the conflict and preparations for war rather than peace would have been important factors that were relevant to your mission and responsibilities both while at the ECMM and Lord Carrington's representative?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I would say that, as I had mentioned before, I didn't feel it was part of my remit to go into the details of weapons and amounts of weapons because I wanted to maintain the trust from all sides. And I would express surprise that this seems to have been organised back in December 1991. Other than that, I really don't have a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There was a reference to secret transactions. Do you feel that the SDA authorities that you were dealing with were keeping this information secret from the international observers?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I don't know how this witness is supposed to speculate about what was in the minds of the SDA leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Please do, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course your contacts with other international monitors, both in the -- both the successors when you left the ECMM and other organisations such as UNPROFOR, and I believe, also at the time there was at least one other mission on the ground, the OSCE, I believe, had a mission as well, did you ever hear from any of them any information of this nature that -- that preparations were made as far as back as December 1991 by the SDA to obtain armaments and prepare for war?

utterances.speaker: COLM MARY DOYLE
utterances.text: No, none of the detail. We assumed that all sides were trying to get weapons because of the fears that were amongst the population. But the detail I have no knowledge of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can now turn to another document, an interview by Mr. -- General Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The document in question is 1D00167 in e-court, and I have just one selection from that document to present to the witness, and that is at page 3 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's the middle of the third paragraph on this page, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The part I want to draw your attention to, it starts off: "From 2nd of December onward, we started organising the rest of the country, and we organised, we established nine regional HQ. Eight besides Sarajevan, 98 municipal HQ, and a number of logistics, the diversionists, entire diversionist units et cetera, the units necessary for waging war. "Before the beginning of the war, we had 126.000 organised men. According to our estimate, although we didn't have exact data, these are the approximate data and they are quite accurate. There were 80.000 armed men. That's the situation by the end of March." Sir, as far as we're still talking about 1991 to March 1992, the period when you were still with the ECMM, to your knowledge, did your monitors report to you of such a situation in the municipalities, that is to say, where the Bosnian Muslim Patriotic League of the SDA had established 98 municipal headquarters and had 80.000 men under arms and 126.000 organised men ready to make war?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we haven't obviously had the luxury of seeing this document until Defence started cross-examining on it, and he just put to the witness that this has to do with the Patriotic League. I can't tell from the excerpt that's on the screen if that's an accurate statement or not of the evidence, and so I see by the time, perhaps we're coming towards the end of the session, if I could have the opportunity to look at the documents obviously overnight, I can indicate whether or not I think the question is fair tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we just got -- the previous document by Mr. Halilovic talked about this. It said that his task was to create headquarters for the Patriotic League, and now he's talking about the number of those headquarters. But I leave it up to Your Honours. It doesn't matter who established them. I'm asking whether this situation was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you even didn't put on the record what kind of document that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... just mentioned a number of a document, but nobody knows what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I mentioned it was being an interview of Mr. Halilovic, Your Honour. I thought I had. I apologise if I had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: An interview to whom? When was it taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would love to know, Your Honour. This is how it was disclosed to us by the Prosecution. Without that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are using it, and we would like to know a little bit more about the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is apparently no translation, Your Honours, into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have heard, Mr. Mladic. The B/C/S booth, can we get help? We are told there is no translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The B/C/S booth is working fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously Madam Bolton says she's seeing this document for the first time, and she would like to be able to make sure that she's on firm ground if she does object or whether she doesn't have an objection to make. It's time to stop. Would that be a convenient time to stop? And we can start with Madam Bolton tomorrow to tell us whether she has gone through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour. I would just only add that since this is a document that came from the Office of the Prosecution, if she could also advise us of its provenance and give us the information that Judge Fluegge was asking for, since that is information that is not in the possession of the Defence and is information that I would be interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure whether, at this stage, when it is now being tendered by the Defence, it's the responsibility of the Prosecution to tell us about its provenance, which provenance was not sought when the document was received by you. I suggest that you sort that out outside court, and if you still need to -- the question of the provenance, we can talk about it tomorrow too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to warn you that you -- we are going to break now until tomorrow. Because you're still in the witness box, you may not discuss the case with anybody, least of all anybody from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Until you are excused from further testifying. As from tomorrow, we are scheduled to start at 9.30 and not at 9.00, so be back here tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning. Same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We stand adjourned to 9.00 -- 9.30 in the morning tomorrow morning. Same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of August, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
